title: Fu-Go balloon bomb

facts.text: The Fu-Go was an unmanned hydrogen balloon about 33 feet (10 meters) across, holding about 19,000 cubic feet of gas when full.
Its envelope was washi paper made from the bark of the kozo, or paper mulberry, bush. Four to five thin layers were glued together.
The glue was a paste made from konnyaku, a starchy root also eaten as food.
Japanese schoolgirls were drafted to make the paper and glue the panels, working long shifts without being told what they were building.
Below the balloon hung a metal ring of sandbags. Barometers fired small charges to drop a sandbag whenever the balloon sank too low, and a valve vented hydrogen if it rose too high.
When the ballast ran out, the ring released the bombs: usually one antipersonnel bomb of about 15 kg and several incendiaries. A final charge was meant to destroy the balloon.
U.S. geologists studied the sand in captured ballast bags and traced it to beaches in Japan.
More than 9,000 were launched from Honshu between 3 November 1944 and April 1945. About 300 were found or seen in North America.
Japan ended the program in April 1945, short of paper and hydrogen and with no word that the balloons had done any damage.

declassified.fact: On 10 March 1945 one balloon drifted into a power line in Washington State that fed the Hanford site, where the Manhattan Project was making plutonium for the atomic bomb. The short circuit cut Hanford's power. It was pure coincidence, since the balloons could not be aimed.
